claim: During embryonic development, radial glial cells give rise to neurons, then to astrocytes following the gliogenic switch.
source: During embryonic development, radial glial cells give rise to neurons, then to astrocytes following the gliogenic switch.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about neural development that is stated in the abstract.

claim: Timely regulation of the gliogenic switch is operated by several transcription factors.
source: Timely regulation of the switch, operated by several transcription factors, is fundamental for allowing coordinated interactions between neurons and glia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about transcriptional regulation of the gliogenic switch.

claim: Deletion of Sox9 early during mouse brain development results in a significantly compromised dentate gyrus.
source: We deleted the gene for one such factor, SOX9, early during mouse brain development and observed a significantly compromised dentate gyrus (DG).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work described in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Previously uncharacterized ALDH1L1+ astrocytic progenitors exist in the cortical hem.
source: We identified in the latter previously uncharacterized ALDH1L1+ astrocytic progenitors, which form a fimbrial-specific glial scaffold necessary for neuronal progenitor migration toward the developing DG.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the study, supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5.

claim: ALDH1L1+ astrocytic progenitors form a fimbrial-specific glial scaffold necessary for neuronal progenitor migration toward the developing DG.
source: We identified in the latter previously uncharacterized ALDH1L1+ astrocytic progenitors, which form a fimbrial-specific glial scaffold necessary for neuronal progenitor migration toward the developing DG.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by lineage tracing and deletion experiments shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: SOX9 plays an early crucial role for DG development through regulation of astroglial potential acquisition in the cortical hem.
source: Our results highlight an early crucial role of SOX9 for DG development through regulation of astroglial potential acquisition in the CH.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study, supported by data showing loss of ALDH1L1+ cells in Sox9 mutants (Figure 5).

claim: Formation of a local network between astrocytic and neuronal progenitors originating from adjacent domains underlies brain morphogenesis.
source: Moreover, we illustrate how formation of a local network, amidst astrocytic and neuronal progenitors originating from adjacent domains, underlays brain morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing interactions between CH-derived astrocytes and DNE-derived neurons.

claim: Neuroepithelial cells are the origin of all neurons, glia and stem cells found in the CNS.
source: Neuroepithelial cells (NECs) are the origin of all neurons, glia and stem cells found in the CNS (Paridaen and Huttner, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Paridaen and Huttner, 2014.

claim: At around E10.5 in the mouse, NECs undergo an irreversible switch, becoming radial glial cells (RGCs).
source: But, at around E10.5 in the mouse, NECs undergo an irreversible switch, becoming radial glial cells (RGCs), which enable them to later generate astrocyte and oligodendrocyte progenitors (Malatesta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about neural development timing, supported by citation to Malatesta et al., 2008.

claim: Spatio-temporal control of the gliogenic switch is crucial because it regulates emergence and abundance of each cell type.
source: Spatio-temporal control of the gliogenic switch is crucial because it regulates emergence and abundance of each cell type, enabling local establishment of fundamental neuron-glia interactions which are necessary for achieving correct CNS cytoarchitecture and functionality (Orduz et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2019; Nichols et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neuron-glia interactions are essential to support the migration of differentiating neurons.
source: Amongst other roles, these interactions are essential to support the migration of differentiating neurons (Cooper, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Cooper, 2013.

claim: RGCs guide migration of their neuronal progeny.
source: RGCs are known to guide migration of their neuronal progeny, while in the adult brain, astrocytes guide neuronal progenitors from the subventricular zone to the olfactory bulb (Lois et al., 1996; Gengatharan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the adult brain, astrocytes guide neuronal progenitors from the subventricular zone to the olfactory bulb.
source: RGCs are known to guide migration of their neuronal progeny, while in the adult brain, astrocytes guide neuronal progenitors from the subventricular zone to the olfactory bulb (Lois et al., 1996; Gengatharan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Lois et al., 1996 and Gengatharan et al., 2016.

claim: Astrocytic commitment has been difficult to monitor in the embryo because specific markers to distinguish these from RGCs were lacking until recently.
source: However, because astrocytic commitment has been difficult to monitor in the embryo, since specific markers to distinguish these from RGCs were lacking until recently (Molofsky et al., 2013; Weng et al., 2019) (notably ALDH1L1, previously known as FDH, 10-formyltetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase [Krupenko, 2009]), a role for astrocytes to support migration in the embryo had not been established (Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the field, supported by citations to Molofsky et al., 2013 and Weng et al., 2019.

claim: ALDH1L1 is a marker that can distinguish astrocytes from RGCs.
source: However, because astrocytic commitment has been difficult to monitor in the embryo, since specific markers to distinguish these from RGCs were lacking until recently (Molofsky et al., 2013; Weng et al., 2019) (notably ALDH1L1, previously known as FDH, 10-formyltetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase [Krupenko, 2009]), a role for astrocytes to support migration in the embryo had not been established (Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A role for astrocytes to support migration in the embryo had not been established prior to this study.
source: However, because astrocytic commitment has been difficult to monitor in the embryo, since specific markers to distinguish these from RGCs were lacking until recently (Molofsky et al., 2013; Weng et al., 2019) (notably ALDH1L1, previously known as FDH, 10-formyltetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase [Krupenko, 2009]), a role for astrocytes to support migration in the embryo had not been established (Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study, supported by citation to Nguyen et al., 2013.

claim: The dentate gyrus is a packed V-shaped layer of granule neurons involved in spatial memory formation and pattern separation.
source: The dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus, is a packed V-shaped layer of granule neurons involved in spatial memory formation and pattern separation (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2020), which hosts a niche of radial glia-like cells supporting adult neurogenesis (Ghosh, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DG anatomy and function, supported by citation to Hainmueller and Bartos, 2020.

claim: The dentate gyrus hosts a niche of radial glia-like cells supporting adult neurogenesis.
source: The dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus, is a packed V-shaped layer of granule neurons involved in spatial memory formation and pattern separation (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2020), which hosts a niche of radial glia-like cells supporting adult neurogenesis (Ghosh, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Ghosh, 2019.

claim: DG granule neuron progenitors originate from the dentate neuroepithelium (DNE) or primary matrix of the archicortex, corresponding to the ventricular zone above the cortical hem.
source: During embryonic development, DG granule neuron progenitors originate from the dentate neuroepithelium (DNE) or primary (1ry) matrix of the archicortex, corresponding to the ventricular zone above the cortical hem (CH; Urbán and Guillemot, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DG development, supported by citation to Urbán and Guillemot, 2014.

claim: From E14.5 in the mouse, pioneer intermediate progenitors, followed by neural stem cells, delaminate to migrate extensively within the parenchyma, along the Dentate Migratory Stream.
source: From E14.5 in the mouse, pioneer intermediate progenitors (IPs), followed by neural stem cells (NSCs), at least some of which will likely form RG-like cells in the adult DG, delaminate to migrate extensively within the parenchyma, along the Dentate Migratory Stream (DMS) or 2ry matrix (Nelson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DG development timing, supported by citation to Nelson et al., 2020.

claim: From E16.5, the mixed cell population of IPs, NSCs, and post-mitotic neurons reaches the brain midline forming the tertiary matrix.
source: From E16.5, this mixed cell population, which also comprises post-mitotic neurons at this stage, ultimately reaches the brain midline forming the 3ry matrix, where they distribute in the upper then lower blades of the DG, and differentiate into PROX1+ granule neurons (Urbán and Guillemot, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DG development, supported by citation to Urbán and Guillemot, 2014.

claim: Cells in the tertiary matrix differentiate into PROX1+ granule neurons.
source: From E16.5, this mixed cell population, which also comprises post-mitotic neurons at this stage, ultimately reaches the brain midline forming the 3ry matrix, where they distribute in the upper then lower blades of the DG, and differentiate into PROX1+ granule neurons (Urbán and Guillemot, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Urbán and Guillemot, 2014.

claim: DG development continues until after birth, when primary and secondary matrices eventually disappear.
source: This process continues until after birth, when 1ry and 2ry matrices eventually disappear, and formation of new granule neurons will exclusively rely on local adult neurogenesis (Nicola et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about postnatal DG development, supported by citation to Nicola et al., 2015.

claim: The cortical hem is a fundamental hippocampal organizer.
source: The CH, which is adjacent to the DNE and subsequently develops into the underlying fimbria, is a fundamental hippocampal organizer (Yoshida et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2006.

claim: The cortical hem gives rise to Cajal-Retzius cells.
source: It gives rise to Cajal-Retzius (CR) cells, which regulate DG progenitor migration via secretion of Reelin and SDF1 (Sibbe et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Sibbe et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Cajal-Retzius cells regulate DG progenitor migration via secretion of Reelin and SDF1.
source: It gives rise to Cajal-Retzius (CR) cells, which regulate DG progenitor migration via secretion of Reelin and SDF1 (Sibbe et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Sibbe et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Progenitor migration along the DMS follows the track of a GFAP+ glial scaffold.
source: Progenitor migration, along the DMS, follows the track of a GFAP+ glial scaffold, which stretches from both the DNE and fimbrial epithelium toward and around the forming DG (Rickmann et al., 1987).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Rickmann et al., 1987.

claim: The GFAP+ glial scaffold stretches from both the DNE and fimbrial epithelium toward and around the forming DG.
source: Progenitor migration, along the DMS, follows the track of a GFAP+ glial scaffold, which stretches from both the DNE and fimbrial epithelium toward and around the forming DG (Rickmann et al., 1987).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Rickmann et al., 1987.

claim: The shape and directionality of GFAP+ filaments within the scaffold suggest a supportive role for progenitor migration.
source: Although definitive proof is lacking, the shape and directionality of GFAP+ filaments within the scaffold suggest a supportive role for progenitor migration, both along the 2ry matrix and within the 3ry matrix (Sibbe et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009; Barry et al., 2008; Piper et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2004; Galichet et al., 2008; Frotscher et al., 2003; Heng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological observations, supported by multiple citations.

claim: GFAP expression suggests that the glial scaffold is formed of differentiating astrocytes.
source: Furthermore, GFAP expression suggests that the glial scaffold is formed of differentiating astrocytes, because GFAP is not expressed in RGCs in rodents (Malatesta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression, supported by citation to Malatesta et al., 2008.

claim: GFAP is not expressed in RGCs in rodents.
source: Furthermore, GFAP expression suggests that the glial scaffold is formed of differentiating astrocytes, because GFAP is not expressed in RGCs in rodents (Malatesta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Malatesta et al., 2008.

claim: Deletion of the genes encoding the transcription factors NF1A/B partly affects formation of the scaffold.
source: Deletion of the genes encoding the transcription factors NF1A/B, which regulate astrocyte gene expression (Kang et al., 2012), partly affects formation of the scaffold, also suggesting an astrocytic contribution (Barry et al., 2008; Piper et al., 2010; Brunne et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Barry et al., 2008; Piper et al., 2010; Brunne et al., 2010.

claim: NF1A/B regulate astrocyte gene expression.
source: Deletion of the genes encoding the transcription factors NF1A/B, which regulate astrocyte gene expression (Kang et al., 2012), partly affects formation of the scaffold, also suggesting an astrocytic contribution (Barry et al., 2008; Piper et al., 2010; Brunne et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Kang et al., 2012.

claim: Direct evidence of astrocytes supporting neuronal progenitor migration during embryonic development has never been reported before this study.
source: However, direct evidence of astrocytes supporting neuronal progenitor migration during embryonic development has never been reported before.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: The glial scaffold has been suggested to have a dual origin with a proximal fimbrial part deriving from the fimbrial glioepithelium, and a distal supragranular domain originating from DNE progenitors.
source: The mechanisms explaining the formation of the scaffold also remain ambiguous: it has been suggested to have a dual origin with a proximal fimbrial part deriving from the fimbrial glioepithelium, and a distal supragranular domain originating from DNE progenitors (Li et al., 2009; Barry et al., 2008; Heng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature, supported by citations to Li et al., 2009; Barry et al., 2008; Heng et al., 2012.

claim: SOX9 starts to be expressed in NECs around E9.5, just before their transition to RGCs and neuro-to-glia switch.
source: SOX9, an SRY-related high mobility group (HMG) box (SOX) transcription factor, starts to be expressed in NECs around E9.5, just before their transition to RGCs and neuro-to-glia switch.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SOX9 expression timing.

claim: SOX9 is required for the neuro-to-glia switch in the embryonic brain.
source: We and others showed that SOX9 is required for this process, both within the embryonic brain (Scott et al., 2010; Hashimoto et al., 2016) and spinal cord (Kang et al., 2012; Stolt et al., 2003), because generation of astrocytes and oligodendrocytes is affected by its deletion.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Scott et al., 2010; Hashimoto et al., 2016.

claim: SOX9 is required for the neuro-to-glia switch in the spinal cord.
source: We and others showed that SOX9 is required for this process, both within the embryonic brain (Scott et al., 2010; Hashimoto et al., 2016) and spinal cord (Kang et al., 2012; Stolt et al., 2003), because generation of astrocytes and oligodendrocytes is affected by its deletion.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Kang et al., 2012; Stolt et al., 2003.

claim: Generation of astrocytes and oligodendrocytes is affected by Sox9 deletion.
source: We and others showed that SOX9 is required for this process, both within the embryonic brain (Scott et al., 2010; Hashimoto et al., 2016) and spinal cord (Kang et al., 2012; Stolt et al., 2003), because generation of astrocytes and oligodendrocytes is affected by its deletion.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Nestin-Cre becomes active from E10.5.
source: However, this Cre-driver only becomes active from E10.5, after the onset of SOX9 expression (Scott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Nestin-Cre line, supported by citation to Scott et al., 2010.

claim: The relatively mild effect of Sox9 loss on astrogenesis in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants might be explained by early, albeit temporary expression of SOX9.
source: Consequently, the relatively mild effect of Sox9 loss on astrogenesis in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants (Kang et al., 2012; Stolt et al., 2003) might also be explained by its early, albeit temporary expression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain observations, with supporting citations.

claim: Sox1Cre is active from E8.5 almost exclusively in the neural tube.
source: To better understand the role of SOX9 in CNS development, including at early stages, we performed conditional deletion using Sox1Cre/+, which is active from E8.5 almost exclusively in the neural tube (Takashima et al., 2007; Wood and Episkopou, 1999), and compared these with Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Sox1Cre line, supported by citations to Takashima et al., 2007; Wood and Episkopou, 1999.

claim: All Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutant mice survived, allowing post-natal analysis.
source: In contrast with the latter model (Tronche et al., 1999), all Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutant mice survived, allowing post-natal analysis.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Reduced DG size was the most prominent defect in adult Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutant brains.
source: Reduced DG size was the most prominent defect in adult Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutant brains, but not in the few surviving Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre animals, and this was already visible in newborns, suggesting an earlier developmental defect.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Reduced DG size was not observed in the few surviving Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre animals.
source: Reduced DG size was the most prominent defect in adult Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutant brains, but not in the few surviving Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre animals, and this was already visible in newborns, suggesting an earlier developmental defect.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Reduced DG size in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants was already visible in newborns.
source: Reduced DG size was the most prominent defect in adult Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutant brains, but not in the few surviving Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre animals, and this was already visible in newborns, suggesting an earlier developmental defect.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: The emergence and differentiation of granule neuron progenitors were not affected in either Sox9 mutant embryos.
source: While the emergence and differentiation of granule neuron progenitors were not affected in either Sox9 mutant embryos, we observed that their migration within the developing DG was compromised, particularly in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Migration of granule neuron progenitors within the developing DG was compromised in Sox9 mutants, particularly in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants.
source: While the emergence and differentiation of granule neuron progenitors were not affected in either Sox9 mutant embryos, we observed that their migration within the developing DG was compromised, particularly in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Formation of the fimbrial glial scaffold was delayed in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants.
source: We then showed that formation of the fimbrial glial scaffold, which is likely supporting neuronal progenitor migration toward the forming DG, was delayed in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Formation of ALDH1L1+ astrocytic progenitors in the CH is significantly compromised in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants.
source: Accordingly, formation of these progenitors is significantly compromised in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, but not in their Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre counterparts, because Nestin-Cre is not active in the CH.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Formation of ALDH1L1+ astrocytic progenitors in the CH is not compromised in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants.
source: Accordingly, formation of these progenitors is significantly compromised in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, but not in their Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre counterparts, because Nestin-Cre is not active in the CH.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Nestin-Cre is not active in the cortical hem.
source: Accordingly, formation of these progenitors is significantly compromised in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, but not in their Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre counterparts, because Nestin-Cre is not active in the CH.
evidence: This is an observation from lineage tracing experiments, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Fimbrial glial scaffold and DG formation are less affected in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants compared to Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants.
source: Consequently, fimbrial glial scaffold and DG formation are less affected in these mutants.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data in Figures 1, 4, and 5.

claim: Exclusive deletion of Sox9 in the CH using Wnt3airesCre confirmed that SOX9 is required for astrocyte progenitor emergence and fimbrial glial scaffold formation.
source: Exclusive deletion of Sox9 in the CH, using Wnt3airesCre (Yoshida et al., 2006), further confirmed that SOX9 is required for astrocyte progenitor emergence and hence fimbrial glial scaffold formation, allowing neuron progenitor migration.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The birth, growth, and survival of Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mice were not overtly affected.
source: The birth, growth, and survival of Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mice were not overtly affected.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: The hippocampus was particularly affected in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ adult brains.
source: However, histological analyses of adult Sox9 mutant brains revealed that the hippocampus was particularly affected (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1i,ii).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The DG emerges as the most affected region in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ adult brains.
source: However, the DG emerges as the most affected region, and quantification of its size shows it was significantly reduced in adult Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mice compared to controls (Figure 1Ai,ii;B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: DG size was significantly reduced in adult Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mice compared to controls.
source: However, the DG emerges as the most affected region, and quantification of its size shows it was significantly reduced in adult Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mice compared to controls (Figure 1Ai,ii;B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by quantitative data in Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of one copy of Sox9 in Sox9fl/+;Sox1Cre/+ mice does not affect DG size.
source: Furthermore, deletion of one copy of Sox9 in Sox9fl/+;Sox1Cre/+ mice does not affect DG size (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The adult DG controls formation of new memories.
source: Because the adult DG controls formation of new memories (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2020), we assessed memory formation abilities in adult Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mice by performing a Novel Object Recognition Test (NORT) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Hainmueller and Bartos, 2020.

claim: Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mice failed to recognize a new object over a familiar one in the Novel Object Recognition Test.
source: Failure to recognise a new object over a familiar one, detected as spending more time to investigate the new object, was demonstrated in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutant mice do not display anxiety-like behavior in the open-field test.
source: This did not reveal any significant difference between control and mutant mice (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Embryonic deletion of Sox9 affects memory-forming abilities.
source: Taken together, these results show that embryonic deletion of Sox9 affects memory-forming abilities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data in Figure 1.

claim: Functionality of DG is affected in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants.
source: This suggests that functionality of DG is affected, albeit we cannot exclude that defects in other regions of the mutant brains explain or exacerbate this behavioral deficiency.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral and anatomical data, with acknowledgment of alternative explanations.

claim: Most Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre animals die at birth.
source: In contrast with Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, most Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre animals die at birth (Scott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Scott et al., 2010.

claim: Activity of Nestin-Cre outside the CNS likely explains mortality in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants.
source: Therefore, activity of Nestin-Cre outside the CNS (Bernal and Arranz, 2018), in tissues where SOX9 is required, such as pancreatic islets (Seymour et al., 2007), heart (Akiyama et al., 2004), and/or kidneys (Reginensi et al., 2011), likely explains mortality in these mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on known Cre activity and SOX9 function, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The size of the DG in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre animals was unaffected both in adults and P2 pups.
source: In contrast with Sox1Cre/+ mutants, the size of the DG in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre animals was unaffected both in adults (Figure 1Aiii,B) and P2 pups (Figure 1Avi,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: At E11.5, eYFP reporter expression was observed throughout the forebrain in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+;R26ReYFP/+ embryos.
source: At E11.5, eYFP reporter expression was observed throughout the forebrain in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+;R26ReYFP/+ embryos (Figure 1Fiii) where, compared to controls, SOX9/Sox9 expression was absent (Figure 1Fii,iv and Figure 1—figure supplement 5Ai–ii,B).
evidence: This is a finding from lineage tracing experiments, supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: SOX9/Sox9 expression was absent in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ embryos at E11.5 compared to controls.
source: At E11.5, eYFP reporter expression was observed throughout the forebrain in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+;R26ReYFP/+ embryos (Figure 1Fiii) where, compared to controls, SOX9/Sox9 expression was absent (Figure 1Fii,iv and Figure 1—figure supplement 5Ai–ii,B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence and ISH, supported by data in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Some rare Sox9-positive cells were detected in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutant archicortices by in situ hybridization.
source: However, in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutant archicortices, we detected some rare Sox9-positive cells by in situ hybridization (arrow in Figure 1—figure supplement 5Aviii, see also Figure 5Gv), demonstrating that recombination of the Sox9 allele is not quite ubiquitous.
evidence: This is a finding from ISH, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and Figure 5G.

claim: Nestin-Cre is only active ventrally at E11.5, gradually progressing dorsally later in gestation.
source: In contrast, Nestin-Cre is only active ventrally at E11.5, gradually progressing dorsally later in gestation (Figure 1Fv–x, Figure 1—figure supplement 5Aiii,vi,ix), as previously shown (Vernay et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a finding from lineage tracing, supported by data in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, and citation to Vernay et al., 2005.

claim: In Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants, SOX9 is transiently expressed in the DNE between E12.5 and E13.5.
source: This implies that in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants, SOX9 is transiently expressed in the DNE between E12.5 and E13.5 (Figure 1Giii,vi).
evidence: This is an inference from the Cre activity pattern, supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: The adjacent CH presents a mosaic pattern of recombination in Nestin-Cre mutants.
source: In addition, the adjacent CH presents a mosaic pattern of recombination in Nestin-Cre mutants (Figure 1Gvi,ix,xii), as previously shown (Li et al., 2009; Winkler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from lineage tracing, supported by data in Figure 1G and citations to Li et al., 2009; Winkler et al., 2018.

claim: Many SOX9-expressing cells can be found at E16.5 in the CH in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants.
source: Consequently, many SOX9-expressing cells can still be found at E16.5 in this region in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants (Figure 1Gxii).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: Delayed recombination in the DNE and/or residual expression of SOX9 in the CH of Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre embryos underlies the difference in adult DG phenotype observed between Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ and Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants.
source: Altogether these results suggest that delayed recombination in the DNE and/or residual expression of SOX9 in the CH of Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre embryos (schematized in Figure 1H) underlies the difference in adult DG phenotype observed between Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ and Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of the two mutant lines.

claim: All three cell types (PAX6+, TBR2+, PROX1+) were found in the same numbers at embryonic stages in both Sox9 mutants compared to controls.
source: All three cell types were found in the same numbers at embryonic stages in both Sox9 mutants compared to controls (Figure 2E,G,J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from cell counting, supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At P2, TBR2+ IPs are reduced in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants compared to controls, with 27.6% fewer cells.
source: However, at P2, TBR2+ IPs are reduced in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants compared to controls, with 27.6% fewer cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a finding from cell counting, supported by quantitative data in Figure 2G.

claim: Analysis of cleaved Caspase-3 immunostaining showed comparable patterns of cell apoptosis between mutants and controls.
source: Analysis of cleaved Caspase-3 immunostaining showed comparable patterns of cell apoptosis between mutants and controls, suggesting Sox9 deletion does not affect progenitor survival at this stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ki67 expression and EdU labeling revealed no difference between controls and mutants in emergence, expansion and differentiation of DG granule neuron progenitors.
source: Moreover, Ki67 expression and EdU labeling, revealed no difference between controls and mutants in emergence, expansion and differentiation of DG granule neuron progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B,D–F,H–J).
evidence: This is a finding from proliferation and birth-dating experiments, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: At E18.5, more TBR2+ cells were found in the 2ry matrix in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants, apparently at the detriment of the 3ry matrix.
source: At E18.5, we counted more TBR2+ cells in the 2ry matrix in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants, apparently at the detriment of the 3ry matrix, where fewer cells were present in both Nestin-Cre and Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants compared to controls (Figure 2Mi).
evidence: This is a finding from cell counting and distribution analysis, supported by data in Figure 2M.

claim: Fewer TBR2+ cells were present in the 3ry matrix of both Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre and Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants at E18.5 compared to controls.
source: At E18.5, we counted more TBR2+ cells in the 2ry matrix in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants, apparently at the detriment of the 3ry matrix, where fewer cells were present in both Nestin-Cre and Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants compared to controls (Figure 2Mi).
evidence: This is a finding from cell counting and distribution analysis, supported by data in Figure 2M.

claim: The misdistribution of TBR2+ cells becomes more evident post-natally.
source: The misdistribution of TBR2+ cells become more evident post-natally, with fewer TBR2+ progenitors in the 3ry matrix of both mutant strains, but with more cells present in the 1ry matrix of Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ embryos and in the 2ry matrix of Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants, compared to controls (Figure 2Mii).
evidence: This is a finding from cell counting and distribution analysis, supported by data in Figure 2M.

claim: In both Sox9 mutants at P2, there was a reduction in PROX1+ differentiating granule neurons in the 3ry matrix and increased number of these cells in the 1ry matrix of Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants.
source: Similarly, in both Sox9 mutants at P2, we observed a reduction in PROX1+ differentiating granule neurons in the 3ry matrix and, in parallel, significantly increased number of these cells in the 1ry matrix of Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants (Figure 2Miii).
evidence: This is a finding from cell counting and distribution analysis, supported by data in Figure 2M.

claim: 1ry-to-2ry matrix distributions of PAX6+ and PAX6+Ki67+ progenitors are not affected in either E14.5 or E16.5 Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants compared to controls.
source: Conversely, 1ry-to-2ry matrix distributions of PAX6+ and PAX6+Ki67+ progenitors (Figure 2LFigure 2—figure supplement 3C) are not affected in either E14.5 or E16.5 Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants compared to controls.
evidence: This is a finding from cell counting and distribution analysis, supported by data in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Defective DG neuronal progenitor distribution in Sox9 mutants arises between E16.5 and E18.5.
source: This suggests that defective DG neuronal progenitor distribution in Sox9 mutants arise between E16.5 and E18.5.
evidence: This is an inference from the temporal analysis of progenitor distribution.

claim: The distribution of PROX1+ cells within the 3ry matrix appears disrupted at E18.5 in both mutants, albeit less severely in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre embryos.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of PROX1+ cells within the 3ry matrix also appears disrupted at E18.5 in both mutants, albeit less severely in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre embryos (Figure 2ii–iii).
evidence: This is a finding from cell distribution analysis, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: In Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, PROX1+ cells accumulate in the lower blade of the developing DG at the detriment of the upper blade.
source: In controls, PROX1+ cells are equally distributed between the upper and lower blade. In contrast, in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, these cells accumulate in the lower blade of the developing DG at the detriment of the upper blade.
evidence: This is a finding from spatial distribution analysis, supported by data in Figure 2N.

claim: An ectopic cluster comprising a mix of both TBR2 and PROX1 expressing cells accumulates close to the ventricle in the developing DG of both Sox9 mutants since E18.5.
source: Furthermore, we noticed in the developing DG of both Sox9 mutants, an ectopic cluster comprising a mix of both TBR2 and PROX1 expressing cells accumulating close to the ventricle since E18.5 (arrows in Figure 2Fii,iii,v,vi,Iv,vi).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 2F and 2I.

claim: Starting from E18.5 progenitors and granule neurons are abnormally distributed in the developing DG of Sox9 mutants, with Sox1Cre mutants being more severely affected.
source: Altogether these analyses show that starting from E18.5 progenitors and granule neurons are abnormally distributed in the developing DG of Sox9 mutants, with Sox1Cre mutants being more severely affected, both along the 1ry-to-3ry matrix axis (Figure 2M) as well as within the forming DG (3ry matrix; Figure 2N).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the cell distribution analyses.

claim: The ectopic cluster is located next to the SOX2+ DNE.
source: It is located next to the SOX2+ DNE (Figure 3Aiv–vi) and contains some SOX2+ progenitors and TBR2+ IPs (some of which are EdU+; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: The ectopic cluster contains some SOX2+ progenitors and TBR2+ IPs.
source: It is located next to the SOX2+ DNE (Figure 3Aiv–vi) and contains some SOX2+ progenitors and TBR2+ IPs (some of which are EdU+; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: Ectopic expression of PROX1 was observed in the ectopic cluster, indicating that some progenitors are locally differentiating in granule neurons at P2.
source: Moreover, we also observed ectopic expression of PROX1 (arrows in Figure 3C) indicating that some progenitors are locally differentiating in granule neurons at this stage.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Cells in the ectopic cluster express NeuroD1 at E18.5, indicating commitment toward a granular cell fate.
source: Their commitment toward a granular cell fate was already visible at E18.5, with cells in the ectopic cluster expressing NeuroD1 (Roybon et al., 2009) (arrows in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 3D and citation to Roybon et al., 2009.

claim: The ectopic cluster comprises cells at different stages of commitment toward the granule neuron fate.
source: In conclusion, the ectopic cluster comprises cells at different stages of commitment toward the granule neuron fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the marker expression analysis in the ectopic cluster.

claim: The ectopic cluster size remained similar in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants at P2 but was significantly decreased in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre animals at the same stage.
source: While this proportion remained similar in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants at P2 (36.7 ± 5.3%), it was significantly decreased in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre animals at the same stage (17.9 ± 3.4%), in agreement with their milder phenotype (Figure 3Ei).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis, supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: The total number of dsRed+ cells within the developing DG at P2 was significantly lower in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants compared to controls.
source: The total number of dsRed+ cells within the developing DG at P2 was significantly lower in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants compared to controls (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a finding from in utero electroporation experiments, supported by data in Figure 3H.

claim: Excess cell death was not observed in electroporated mutants compared either to the contralateral side, or to controls at P2.
source: We did not observe excess cell death in electroporated mutants compared either to the contralateral side, or to controls at this stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from apoptosis analysis, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In P2 controls, the highest proportion of dsRed+ cells was observed in the 3ry matrix.
source: In P2 controls, the highest proportion of dsRed+ cells was observed in the 3ry matrix (51.27 ± 14.20%), demonstrating that an important fraction of E15.5 electroporated progenitors had given rise to migrating granule neurons that successfully reached their destination in the developing DG (Figure 3G,J, arrowheads in G).
evidence: This is a finding from in utero electroporation experiments, supported by data in Figure 3G and 3J.

claim: In Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, the highest proportion of dsRed+ cells was found in the 2ry matrix.
source: In contrast, in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, the highest proportion of dsRed+ cells was found in the 2ry matrix (39.18 ± 13.59%) and the fraction of cells remaining in the 1ry matrix was significantly higher than in controls (Figure 3G,J).
evidence: This is a finding from in utero electroporation experiments, supported by data in Figure 3G and 3J.

claim: In Sox9 mutants, a proportion of electroporated progenitors remained trapped near the DNE.
source: This suggests that, in Sox9 mutants, a proportion of electroporated progenitors remained trapped near the DNE (arrow in Figure 3Gii).
evidence: This is an inference from the distribution of electroporated cells, supported by data in Figure 3G.

claim: Expression of chemokines (Reln, Cxcl12) and their receptors (Vldlr, Cxcr4) is not significantly different in Sox9 mutant E12.5 dissected archicortices compared to controls.
source: Expression of chemokines (Reln, Cxcl12) and their receptors (Vldlr, Cxcr4) known to be involved in early stages of DG progenitor migration (Frotscher et al., 2003; Mimura-Yamamoto et al., 2017), is not significantly different in Sox9 mutant E12.5 dissected archicortices compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from qPCR analysis, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At E18.5, REELIN expression pattern and intensity appeared unchanged in both Sox9 mutants compared to controls.
source: Similarly, at E18.5, REELIN expression pattern and intensity appeared unchanged in both Sox9 mutants compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) further suggesting that Cajal-Retzius (CR) cells are not affected by loss of Sox9.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A strongly positive GFAP+ scaffold was observed in control samples from E18.5 connecting the DNE to the forming DG, through the fimbria.
source: We thus examined expression of GFAP and observed a strongly positive scaffold in control samples from E18.5 connecting the DNE to the forming DG, through the fimbria (Figure 4Ai,B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: The GFAP+ scaffold is almost absent in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ embryos at E18.5.
source: In contrast, this is almost absent in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ (Figure 4Aii) but only partially affected in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre embryos (quantified in Figure 4C), where the supragranular glial scaffold is missing, but the fimbrial glial scaffold is still visible (inset Figure 4Aiii; see schematic B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 4A and 4C.

claim: The GFAP+ scaffold is only partially affected in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre embryos at E18.5, where the supragranular glial scaffold is missing, but the fimbrial glial scaffold is still visible.
source: In contrast, this is almost absent in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ (Figure 4Aii) but only partially affected in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre embryos (quantified in Figure 4C), where the supragranular glial scaffold is missing, but the fimbrial glial scaffold is still visible (inset Figure 4Aiii; see schematic B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 4A and 4C.

claim: GFAP expression and scaffold structure in both Sox9 mutants partially recover by P2.
source: GFAP expression and scaffold structure in both Sox9 mutants partially recover by P2 (Figure 4Aiv–vi, quantified in C), suggesting that absence of SOX9 might only delay scaffold formation, and that either compensatory or independent mechanisms may allow recovery early post-natally.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 4A and 4C.

claim: Absence of SOX9 might only delay scaffold formation, and compensatory or independent mechanisms may allow recovery early post-natally.
source: GFAP expression and scaffold structure in both Sox9 mutants partially recover by P2 (Figure 4Aiv–vi, quantified in C), suggesting that absence of SOX9 might only delay scaffold formation, and that either compensatory or independent mechanisms may allow recovery early post-natally.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the recovery of GFAP expression.

claim: The impact of delayed scaffold formation on DG morphogenesis is permanent.
source: However, the impact on DG morphogenesis is permanent.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the observation that adult DG size remains reduced despite scaffold recovery.

claim: Close to the DNE, the GFAP+ fimbrial scaffold appears well separated from both the intermediate DNE progenitors and those migrating in the 2ry matrix.
source: Close to the DNE, the GFAP+ fimbrial scaffold appears well separated from both the intermediate DNE progenitors and those migrating in the 2ry matrix (Figure 4Fa).
evidence: This is a finding from 3D reconstruction analysis, supported by data in Figure 4F and Video 1.

claim: Along the migratory stream in the 2ry matrix, progenitors start being more closely associated with the GFAP+ scaffold.
source: Along the migratory stream in the 2ry matrix, progenitors start being more closely associated with the GFAP+ scaffold (Figure 4Fb).
evidence: This is a finding from 3D reconstruction analysis, supported by data in Figure 4F and Video 2.

claim: From the distal part of the fimbria, progenitors and scaffold appear completely intermingled.
source: Finally, from the distal part of the fimbria, progenitors and scaffold appear completely intermingled (Figure 4Fc).
evidence: This is a finding from 3D reconstruction analysis, supported by data in Figure 4F and Video 3.

claim: In the 3ry matrix, IPs and the GFAP supragranular scaffold appear closely associated.
source: We observe a similar association in the 3ry matrix between IPs and the GFAP supragranular scaffold (Figure 4Fd).
evidence: This is a finding from 3D reconstruction analysis, supported by data in Figure 4F and Video 4.

claim: The position of IPs relative to the glial scaffold suggests close contacts between these cell populations, supporting a functional role for the glial scaffold in promoting progenitor migration.
source: The position of IPs relative to the glial scaffold suggest close contacts between these cell populations, supporting a functional role for the glial scaffold in promoting progenitor migration, particularly within the 2ry matrix.
evidence: This is an inference from the spatial relationship observed in 3D reconstructions.

claim: Delayed formation of the glial scaffold in Sox9 mutants is likely implicated in the defective migration of DG progenitor.
source: Consequently, delayed formation of the glial scaffold in Sox9 mutants is likely implicated in the defective migration of DG progenitor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between scaffold defects and migration defects.

claim: SOX9 directly regulates the expression of Gfap in the developing spinal cord.
source: Because SOX9 directly regulates the expression of Gfap in the developing spinal cord (Kang et al., 2012), absence of GFAP expression in Sox9 mutants may simply reflect downregulation of the gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Kang et al., 2012.

claim: At E18.5, ALDH1L1 expression pattern overlaps with that of GFAP, particularly within the fimbria.
source: At E18.5, ALDH1L1 expression pattern overlaps with that of GFAP, particularly within the fimbria where we see many GFAP+; ALDH1L1+ fibers (arrowheads in inset b in Figure 5Ai).
evidence: This is a finding from double immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: GFAP+ALDH1L1- fibers are observed around the developing DG at E18.5.
source: In contrast, we observe GFAP+ALDH1L1- fibers around the developing DG (arrowheads in inset a in Figure 5Ai).
evidence: This is a finding from double immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: At E16.5, before upregulation of GFAP, the ALDH1L1 expression pattern is reminiscent of that at E18.5, as mostly confined to the fimbria.
source: At E16.5, before upregulation of GFAP, the ALDH1L1 expression pattern is reminiscent of that at E18.5, as mostly confined to the fimbria (Figure 5Aii).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: ALDH1L1+ cells are found as early as E13.5 in the archicortex.
source: ALDH1L1+ cells are found as early as E13.5 in the archicortex (Figure 5Aiii) and also at this stage, they are specifically localized in the LEF1-negative;SOX2high CH (Sugiyama et al., 2013; Figure 5B,Ci–ii).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: ALDH1L1+ cells are specifically localized in the LEF1-negative;SOX2high CH at E13.5.
source: ALDH1L1+ cells are found as early as E13.5 in the archicortex (Figure 5Aiii) and also at this stage, they are specifically localized in the LEF1-negative;SOX2high CH (Sugiyama et al., 2013; Figure 5B,Ci–ii).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 5B and 5C, and citation to Sugiyama et al., 2013.

claim: BLBP and GLAST, known markers of astrocytic progenitors, are also present within the LEF1-negative; SOX2high CH.
source: The astrocytic nature of ALDH1L1+ cells was further confirmed by stainings for BLBP and GLAST, known markers of astrocytic progenitors (Nagao et al., 2016) which are also present within the LEF1-negative; SOX2high CH (Figure 5Ciii,iv).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 5C and citation to Nagao et al., 2016.

claim: Astrocytic progenitors are confined to the CH/fimbria throughout development.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that astrocytic progenitors are confined to the CH/fimbria throughout development suggesting they might later give rise to the fimbrial glial scaffold.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial and temporal expression patterns of astrocytic markers.

claim: There was a dramatic reduction in the number of ALDH1L1+ cells in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants compared to controls, both at E13.5 and E16.5.
source: Strikingly, there was a dramatic reduction in their number in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants compared to controls, both at E13.5 and E16.5 (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is a finding from cell counting, supported by data in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Aldh1l1 expression was significantly reduced in dissected archicortices of Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ E12.5 embryos compared to controls.
source: Accordingly, Aldh1l1 expression was significantly reduced in dissected archicortices of Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ E12.5 embryos compared to controls (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a finding from qPCR analysis, supported by data in Figure 5F.

claim: SOX9 is required for the emergence of astrocytic ALDH1L1+ progenitors.
source: This is consistent with a requirement for SOX9 for the emergence of astrocytic ALDH1L1+ progenitors, and consequently formation of the GFAP+ glial scaffold.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the loss of ALDH1L1+ cells in Sox9 mutants.

claim: ALDH1L1+ cell number was unaffected in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants.
source: In contrast to Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, ALDH1L1+ cell number was unaffected in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is a finding from cell counting and qPCR, supported by data in Figure 5D-F.

claim: At E13.5, ALDH1L1+ cells were expressing SOX9 in the CH of Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre embryos.
source: At E13.5, ALDH1L1+ cells were expressing SOX9 in the CH of Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre embryos (Figure 5Gii,vi), and this was still observed at E16.5 (Figure 5Giv,viii).
evidence: This is a finding from double immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 5G.

claim: Some rare SOX9+ cells were present in the CH of E13.5 Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, and some were ALDH1L1+.
source: Interestingly, some rare SOX9+ cells were also present in the CH of E13.5 Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants, and some were ALDH1L1+ (Figure 5Gi,v).
evidence: This is a finding from double immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 5G.

claim: In the CH of Sox9 mutants, ALDH1L1+ cells may only arise from SOX9+ progenitors that escaped Cre recombination.
source: These results suggest that in the CH of Sox9 mutants, ALDH1L1+ cells may only arise from SOX9+ progenitors that escaped Cre recombination, which are present in higher numbers in Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre compared to Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ mutants (schematized in Figure 5H).
evidence: This is an inference from the co-expression analysis of SOX9 and ALDH1L1.

claim: The correlation between the extent of ALDH1L1+ cells and fimbrial glial scaffold loss with the severity of the progenitor migration defect suggests a supporting migratory role of the scaffold.
source: Moreover, the correlation between the extent of ALDH1L1+ cells and fimbrial glial scaffold loss with the severity of the progenitor migration defect in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ versus Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants, further suggests a supporting migratory role of the scaffold.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparative analysis of the two mutant lines.

claim: In the developing spinal cord, the expression of the transcription factors NF1A/B are regulated by SOX9 and this is important for astrocytic differentiation.
source: Finally, in the developing spinal cord, the expression of the transcription factors NF1A/B are regulated by SOX9 and this is important for astrocytic differentiation (Kang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Kang et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of SOX9 does not affect either NF1A/B protein or transcript levels in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ E12.5 embryos.
source: We thus examined expression of NF1A and B in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ E12.5 embryos. Both genes are expressed in the archicortex in control embryos. Loss of SOX9 does not affect either NF1A/B protein or transcript levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence and qPCR, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Distinct molecular mechanisms downstream of SOX9 must underlie astrocytic specification in different domains of the CNS.
source: We conclude that distinct molecular mechanisms downstream of SOX9 must underlie astrocytic specification in different domains of the CNS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential regulation of NF1A/B in spinal cord versus forebrain.

claim: eYFP staining is mostly confined to the LEF1- CH at E12.5 in Wnt3airesCre;R26ReYFP/+ embryos.
source: In Wnt3airesCre;R26ReYFP/+ embryos, eYFP staining is mostly confined to the LEF1- CH at E12.5 (Figure 6Ai–iii) and to CH-derived REELIN+ CR cells both around the DG (Figure S.12.Ai-iv) and in the outer layer of the cortex (Figure 6—figure supplement 1Av–viii).
evidence: This is a finding from lineage tracing, supported by data in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A few YFP+ cells were observed in the LEF1+ DNE, suggesting partial Wnt3airesCre recombination in the DNE.
source: Because a few YFP+ cells were observed in the LEF1+ DNE, suggesting partial Wnt3airesCre recombination in the DNE (arrowheads in Figure 6Ai–iii), we analyzed YFP expression in granule neurons at P2.
evidence: This is a finding from lineage tracing, supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Only 6.45 ± 1% of PROX1+ granule neurons were YFP+ at P2 in Wnt3airesCre;R26ReYFP/+ embryos.
source: Only 6.45 ± 1% of PROX1+ granule neurons were YFP+ at this stage (arrowheads in Figure 6Bi–iii), suggesting Wnt3airesCre is a suitable Cre driver for CH-specific deletion of Sox9.
evidence: This is a finding from lineage tracing, supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: At P2, the fimbrial glial scaffold is entirely eYFP+ in Wnt3airesCre;R26ReYFP/+ embryos.
source: At P2, the fimbrial glial scaffold is entirely eYFP+ (arrowheads in Figure 6Biv–vi).
evidence: This is a finding from lineage tracing, supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: Some GFAP+;eYFP- filaments were observed in the DNE that may represent DNE-derived RGCs.
source: We also observed some GFAP+;eYFP- filaments in the DNE that may represent DNE-derived RGCs (arrows in Figure 6Biv–vi).
evidence: This is a finding from lineage tracing with interpretation, supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: The supragranular glial scaffold is made of both eYFP+ and eYFP- fibers suggesting a dual DNE and CH origin.
source: Conversely, the supragranular glial scaffold is made of both eYFP+ and eYFP- fibers suggesting a dual DNE and CH origin (arrowheads and arrows in Figure 6Bvii–ix, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from lineage tracing, supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: The fimbrial glial scaffold is entirely derived from CH ALDH1L1+ astrocytic progenitors.
source: Altogether these results suggest that the fimbrial glial scaffold is entirely derived from CH ALDH1L1+ astrocytic progenitors, while the supragranular glial scaffold only partially originates from CH.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the lineage tracing experiments.

claim: No PDGFRa+ oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) were observed in the progeny of CH Wnt3airesCre cells.
source: Additionally, we did not observe any PDGFRa+ oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in the progeny of CH Wnt3airesCre cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) arguing in favor of an astrocytic, rather than radial-glial, nature of the scaffold.
evidence: This is a finding from lineage tracing, supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants died shortly after birth.
source: While we were able to harvest mutant embryos until E18.5, animals died shortly after birth, precluding any postnatal analyses.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Deletion of Sox9 in the embryonic heart, skeleton, pancreas, and kidney is known to result in postnatal lethality.
source: Wnt3a is widely expressed in embryonic mesoderm precursors (Takada et al., 1994) and deletion of Sox9 in the embryonic heart, skeleton, pancreas, and kidney is known to result in postnatal lethality (Seymour et al., 2007; Akiyama et al., 2004; Reginensi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Seymour et al., 2007; Akiyama et al., 2004; Reginensi et al., 2011.

claim: In Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutant CNS, SOX9 is absent specifically in the CH at E13.5.
source: In Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutant CNS, SOX9 is absent specifically in the CH at E13.5 (Figure 6Ci–iv).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 6C.

claim: There was a 50% reduction of ALDH1L1+ cells in the CH in E13.5 Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants compared to controls.
source: Importantly, we also observe a 50% reduction of ALDH1L1+ cells in this area in E13.5 mutants compared to controls (Figure 6Cv,vi; quantified in D).
evidence: This is a finding from cell counting, supported by data in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: At E18.5, the GFAP+ fimbrial glial scaffold is exclusively compromised in Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants.
source: Interestingly, at E18.5, the GFAP+ fimbrial glial scaffold is exclusively compromised in Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants (star in Figure 6Cviii), while the supragranular one is unaffected.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 6C.

claim: The supragranular glial scaffold is unaffected in Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants at E18.5.
source: Interestingly, at E18.5, the GFAP+ fimbrial glial scaffold is exclusively compromised in Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants (star in Figure 6Cviii), while the supragranular one is unaffected.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 6C.

claim: GFAP expression is significantly reduced in the fimbrial scaffold in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ and Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants, compared to controls, but not when Nestin-Cre is used to delete Sox9.
source: This analysis clearly shows that GFAP expression is significantly reduced in the fimbrial scaffold, in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ and Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants, compared to controls, but not when Nestin-Cre is used to delete Sox9. (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis, supported by data in Figure 6F.

claim: GFAP expression in the supragranular scaffold is reduced in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ and Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants compared to controls, but not in Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants.
source: Conversely, GFAP expression in the supragranular scaffold, is reduced in Sox9fl/fl;Sox1Cre/+ and Sox9fl/fl;Nestin-Cre mutants compared to controls, but not in Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants.
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis, supported by data in Figure 6F.

claim: SOX9 is required in the CH for specification of the ALDH1L1+ astrocytic progenitors giving rise to GFAP+ fimbrial glial scaffold.
source: These results are consistent with the differential activity pattern of the Cre drivers. Moreover, they confirm a role for SOX9 in the CH for specification of the ALDH1L1+ astrocytic progenitors giving rise to GFAP+ fimbrial glial scaffold.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the CH-specific deletion experiments.

claim: The normal appearance of the supragranular glial scaffold in Sox9fl/fl;Wnt3airesCre/+ mutants is consistent with the observation that it may have a dual CH and DNE origin.
